modifier.description:
Value type modifier

Non empty constraint is specified by adding an exclamation mark in front of the ValueType:
```type
  where: !Location
```

The desire to preserve empty values (such that they can be differentiated from the lack of any value) is specified
by adding a question mark in front of the ValueType:
```type
  approved: ?boolean
```

The non optional function parameter constraint is specified by adding `!?` in front of the ValueType:
```type
  f: function(url: !?string serialized Url)
```

@see #isNonEmpty
@see #preservesEmpty
@see #isNonOptionalParam
@see FunctionParam#isNonOptional

fieldTypes.description: The declared field types. For simple tuples, this will never be empty but for named tuples with mixins it may be.

title:
"Tuples" are simple structures that don't require a full type declaration. They are useful to declare structure for
a function parameter without having to define a type for that single use.

Tuples can either be named or not. If named, the syntax uses braces like a JSON object:
```type
{ key: string, count: int, dim: Dimension }
```
This kind of tuple can be thought of as an anonymous type, with only data fields.

If unnamed, it uses parenthesis like Python:
```type
(string, int, Dimension)
```
This kind of tuple can be thought of as an array of fixed length with different types specified for each element.

Note that if the tuple has only a single type, use a trailing comma: `(string,)` (again like Python).

It is also possible to declare an _any tuple_ using the `tuple` syntax. These refer to any type of tuple (named or
unnamed and with any set of fields). Of course, instances of abstract tuples are not possible, but instance of any
concrete tuple type will be allowed.

Note that tuples are not easily reusable nor can they have methods, so they're not a good choice for something
like a "complex number" which should be both. If you find yourself using the same tuple declaration multiple times,
that suggests a type might be preferable.
name: TupleType
